item.title: China names 815 athletes for Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
Members of Chinese delegation for the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games attend the inaugural meeting of Chinese delegation for the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 4, 2026. (Xinhua/Wang Dongzhen) BEIJING, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- China announced on Friday its 1,274-member delegation for the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, with 815 athletes set to compete across 38 sports and 369 events. Led by 36 Olympic champions, the squad has an average age of 24. Over a quarter of the athletes are 20 or under and most will be making their Asian Games debuts. Among the team staff, there are 69 overseas specialists from 24 countries and regions including Australia, Spain, France, the Netherlands and Britain. "The Asian Games represents the highest-level comprehensive sporting event in Asia and serves as a genuine test of our preparation," diver Wang Zongyuan said on behalf of the athletes. "We will showcase China's standard and strength on the regional and global stage." "Since 1982, China has topped both the gold medal and overall medal tables at 11 consecutive Asian Games editions," said Gao Zhidan, director of the China's General Administration of Sport and chef de mission of China's delegation, adding that China will strive to maintain its leading position at the Games. The 2026 Asian Games will run from September 19 to October 4, featuring 43 sports and athletes from 45 countries and regions. ■ Shi Zhiyong, representative of coaches, speaks during the inaugural meeting of Chinese delegation for the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 4, 2026. item.title: China to expand health insurance coverage for innovative drugs
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
BEIJING, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- China will expand national health insurance coverage for innovative drugs used to treat cancer, chronic and rare diseases, and childhood illnesses, with the goal of easing the financial burden on patients and their families. Since 2018, China has added 949 medicines to its national health insurance drug list, including 199 innovative drugs, Li Tao, deputy head of the National Healthcare Security Administration, said at a news conference on Friday. The administration plans to expand the range of innovative drugs covered by commercial health insurance. It will encourage commercial insurers to step in first to cover drugs that are not included in the basic health insurance program but offer significant clinical benefits and address important medical needs. It will also shorten approval timelines and help bring pharmaceutical innovations into clinical use more quickly, Li said. China's innovative pharmaceutical sector has grown rapidly in recent years. By 2025, China accounted for about 30 percent of the global biopharma pipeline, up from just 2 percent a decade earlier, and about one-fifth of global licensing deals, according to McKinsey research. In the first half of 2026, the total value of China's innovative drug out-licensing deals reached a record high of more than 100 billion U.S. dollars, according to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology. ■

item.title: Factbox: Latest relief and rescue progress at mudslide-hit border port in China's Xizang
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
BEIJING, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- A fast-moving chain mudslide, triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal, struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region on Aug. 26, causing heavy casualties and leaving many missing. Chinese rescuers immediately launched all-out search and rescue operations. Here is what we know about the deadly mudslide and the latest progress in China: -- Twenty-one people have been confirmed dead and 541 others remain missing after the mudslide struck the border port, according to the regional government's latest news briefing. An ice-rock avalanche originating from a high-mountain glacier in Nepal has been identified as the cause of the mudslide. -- Power supply has been restored to the core area of the mudslide-hit Gyirong Port, the State Grid said. -- After the land route along to Gyirong Port was basically restored on Wednesday morning, large machinery is being used to clear obstacles and create working areas, followed closely by specialized firefighters conducting targeted searches and life-detection equipment verifying suspicious locations. -- More than 2,300 rescuers had been deployed. Multiple rounds of grid and blanket searches have been completed, covering a total area of about 1.59 million square meters. -- In the core affected area, a cumulative total of 336 rescuers have conducted multiple rounds of exhaustive searches, ensuring thorough coverage of every section. -- Rescuers are also collecting and registering all suspected personal belongings of the deceased and the missing to facilitate identification and handover. As of Wednesday noon, 847 items had been recovered. -- The Ministry of Emergency Management, in coordination with the Ministry of Transport, has dispatched road-reinforcement and heavy-lift equipment to the site. -- Central state-owned enterprises have mobilized personnel and machinery to the core area, working to secure power supply and support relief operations, according to the State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission. -- Another batch of Chinese relief supplies and DNA experts arrived in Kathmandu, Nepal, by air on Thursday, as part of Chinese aid efforts following the deadly mudslide. ■

item.title: Direct Beijing-Bucharest-Zagreb flight opens new gateway to Central, Eastern Europe
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
* Air China now serves 27 European destinations with nearly 260 weekly flights between the two continents, with the Beijing-Bucharest-Zagreb route adding another thread to this growing network. * For Croatia, where tourism accounts for about one-fifth of GDP, the direct flight is a long-awaited gateway to the world's largest outbound tourism market. For Romania, it restores a connection that has been absent since 2003. And for Chinese travelers, it offers a new, hassle-free entry point to the wider Balkan region. by Xinhua writers Yao Yulin, Ma Zhen and Li Xuejun BUCHAREST/ZAGREB, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Air China launched its maiden Beijing-Bucharest-Zagreb flight on Friday, restoring direct passenger links between China and Romania after more than two decades and inaugurating the first-ever scheduled passenger service between China and Croatia. Operating three times a week, the new route comes as Central and Eastern Europe -- known for its Adriatic coastline, medieval towns and rich cultural heritage -- is attracting growing interest from Chinese travelers. Travel has become more convenient than ever following China's unilateral visa-free policy for ordinary citizens of both Romania and Croatia. For Croatia, where tourism accounts for about one-fifth of GDP, the direct flight is a long-awaited gateway to the world's largest outbound tourism market. For Romania, it restores a connection that has been absent since 2003. And for Chinese travelers, it offers a new, hassle-free entry point to the wider Balkan region. VISA-FREE BENEFITS China and Romania once enjoyed direct air links, with Air China operating the route until 1994 and Romania's TAROM taking over until its suspension in 2003. For the next 23 years, travelers had to transit through third countries, turning a straightforward journey into a half-day ordeal. The new Beijing-Bucharest-Zagreb route has finally restored that missing link. The timing is no coincidence. In November 2024, China expanded its unilateral visa-free policy to include Romania and Croatia, along with seven other countries. Ordinary passport holders from both nations can now stay in China for up to 30 days without a visa for tourism, business, family visits or transit. The results have been striking. Around 35,000 Romanian citizens traveled to China in 2024, twice the figure recorded a year earlier. In the first seven months of 2025 alone, nearly 36,000 Romanians visited China, up 78 percent year-on-year, according to the National Association of Travel Agencies in Romania. Dan-Horia Maxim, Romania's ambassador to China, described the restored direct flights as "a major diplomatic and economic success aimed at bringing our communities closer together" in a press release. Chen Feng, China's ambassador to Romania, told Xinhua that the resumption of regular direct passenger flights has been a shared aspiration of the Chinese and Romanian peoples and reflects sustained joint efforts on both sides. "It is expected to help further strengthen bilateral economic and trade cooperation, deepen cultural and people-to-people exchanges, promote mutual understanding, and inject fresh momentum into the sustained and healthy development of China-Romania relations," Chen added. For Croatia, the numbers tell a story of promise still waiting to be fulfilled. In 2024, the country welcomed over 250,475 Chinese tourist arrivals, up more than 41 percent from the previous year. Yet that figure remains barely half of the pre-pandemic peak of some 490,000. Industry insiders view the new air link as a key step toward unlocking further growth. Qi Qianjin, China's ambassador to Croatia, called the route "the first direct flight in the history of the two countries and the latest achievement in deepening bilateral relations," adding that it would "significantly reduce travel time and costs, further unleash cooperation potential, and promote exchanges in trade, tourism, culture, sports and people-to-people ties." For China, the route fits into a broader pattern of deepening air connectivity with Central and Eastern Europe. Air China now serves 27 European destinations with nearly 260 weekly flights between the two continents, with the Beijing-Bucharest-Zagreb route adding another thread to this growing network. BALKAN HUB Kristjan Stanicic, director of the Croatian National Tourist Board (CNTB), described the air link as "an important step forward" that "opens up additional opportunities for Croatian tourism to position itself more strongly on the large and promising Chinese market." He said Croatia is reaching out to Chinese visitors "through its exceptional diversity, but also through an authentic experience of our country, the local way of life, tradition and values." The CNTB, through its Shanghai office, plans to continue working with Chinese partners to "enable Chinese guests to get to know our homeland, its heritage and people in a quality and deeper way," Stanicic added. Dubrovnik, Split, Zadar and the capital Zagreb remain among the most popular Croatian destinations for Chinese tourists, but industry observers believe the new route could broaden that map. Leon Jiang, president of the Balkan Chinese Tourism Association and the Croatian Chinese Tourists Guide Association, said that direct access eliminates the inconvenience of transfers, making travel easier for both Chinese tourists heading to the Adriatic and Croatians interested in visiting China. Romania, too, stands to benefit significantly from the restored air link as the new route responds to long-standing calls from the tourism industry and provides infrastructure to meet growing two-way travel demand. In the first half of 2025 alone, Romania welcomed 21,682 Chinese tourists, the highest number of Asian visitors on record. With direct flights now in operation, the bottleneck that once held back the market's full potential is being removed. Romania has been actively positioning itself to capture a larger share of the Chinese outbound market. In May, Romania made its debut at ITB China in Shanghai, one of the most important B2B travel trade events dedicated to the Chinese market. The delegation promoted destinations including Bucharest, Transylvania and the monasteries of Bucovina. Earlier in October 2025, the China Tourism Fair was held at the Chinese Cultural Center in Bucharest, bringing together over 100 representatives from the tourism, culture and education sectors of both countries. Zagreb's strategic location also gives the route broader regional significance. Ljubo Jurcic, professor of economics and former Croatian minister of economy, pointed out that Chinese travelers arriving in Zagreb can easily continue to Italy and Austria, while the Adriatic coast is only a short journey away. Jurcic added that the route also signals Chinese interest in expanding cooperation with Croatia beyond tourism. "Croatian business people have long considered China an interesting market, because China is today the largest and most influential country in the world when it comes to business," he said. "Unfortunately, Croatian business people were not turned to China in time, but today that is changing." ■

Chinese President Xi Jinping paid a state visit to Egypt from Tuesday to Wednesday after attending the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Summit 2026 in Bishkek, and concluding his state visit to Kyrgyzstan. item.title: China ensures lawful rights of foreign nationals involved in criminal cases in China: spokesperson
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
BEIJING, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Friday that China ensures lawful rights of foreign nationals suspected of criminal activities in China. Guo made the remarks on a daily news briefing when asked to comment on a statement released by Singapore's foreign ministry, stating that 52 Singaporeans were arrested in China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region following a law enforcement operation against suspected pyramid scheme activities. "China handles cases involving illegal or criminal activities by foreign nationals on Chinese soil in accordance with the law and ensures that their lawful rights are fully protected," Guo said. ■

item.title: Letter from Gyirong: Mud, loss, scouring, a night in the heart of disaster
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
by Xinhua writer Jigme Dorje GYIRONG, Xizang, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- As dusk settled on Aug. 31, our helicopter arrived at the destination. I jumped from the hovering aircraft a few meters above the ground, clutching my camera bag tightly against my chest, into a vast stretch of mud. Here I was, right in the heart of the disaster-hit zone, five days after a fast-moving chain mudslide, triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal, struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region on Aug. 26, claiming 21 lives and leaving 541 others missing as of midday Sept. 2. I came with a colleague. As a photojournalist, reporting from the scene is my professional calling. The moment my feet touched the ground, they sank deep into the mud. My legs were locked in place, while my upper body swayed for a moment before I regained my balance. A moment before, as the helicopter was descending, I looked through the window and saw what appeared to be a stretch of flat ground completely covered in mud. Only after landing did I realize just how deep it was. I tried to pull my legs free. The mud seemed to pull back. I struggled for a while, but could barely move. We were among the few reporters flown by helicopter directly into the disaster zone. At that time, the overland route into the core affected area remained inaccessible due to serious damages caused by the mudslide. Excavators were working around the clock to clear and reopen the lifeline. The first team of 141 rescuers, as well as a high-altitude helicopter, arrived at the port on the morning of Aug. 27. The next day, two teams, comprising 21 people and a search dog, became the first professional rescue teams to reach the core rescue zone at the border gate. "You're reporters, right?" a firefighter asked. "This is the last helicopter today. You're not going back tonight?" "Yes," I told him. "We're reporters." When I looked around, it struck me that I had lost count of how many times I had been to Gyirong Port. One visit remains particularly vivid in my memory. On that trip, I stayed at a small guesthouse run by villagers in Jifu Village, halfway up a mountain in Gyirong Town. I woke up the next morning to the chirping of birds. Still half asleep, I looked out the window to see a sea of clouds stretching across the valley below. I could hear people chatting and laughing nearby, including a Nepali staff member speaking Mandarin in a slightly halting voice. That was Gyirong Port as I remembered it. Now, in the middle of the devastated landscape, a square concrete platform appeared to be the only remaining structure left visible. It was the reservoir that had supplied drinking water to port staff members and residents. On the lid of the former reservoir, covering several dozen square meters, firefighters who had been among the first to reach the disaster zone had pitched a small red tent. It was barely large enough for the temporary camp of more than a dozen firefighters. With a shovel in hand, my colleague and I dug out a patch of relatively level ground beside the firefighters' tent, just large enough for a single-person tent. That was where we spent the night. Then we picked up our cameras and got back to work. Rescuers were spread across the disaster zone, searching through the mud. We interviewed and photographed several of them as they worked. As darkness fell, rescuers gradually returned to the tents, exhausted. I looked toward the foot of the mountain. One rescuer was still there, head bowed, moving slowly through the darkness, searching. By 9 p.m., it was completely dark. More and more rescuers returned to the camp to rest. Some sat down and began scraping mud from their boots. When an ethnic Tibetan firefighter sat down and pulled off his socks, we saw that his feet had been soaked in muddy water for so long that the skin had turned pale and wrinkled. Heavy machinery rumbled through the night, clearing and repairing the road, while the headlamps of crews working to restore power and communications flickered continuously in the distance. The rescuers were getting ready to eat and invited us to join them. They had pan-fried buns with braised meat. Drones had been employed to air-drop supplies to these rescuers. "This is our first meal today," an immigration police officer said. As we talked, they recalled what had happened the night before. A huge boulder had fallen from the mountain across the Gyirong Zangbo River. They had heard a deep, muffled cracking sound. Then came a loud crash as the rock plunged into the river. "The noise was enormous," one of the rescuers said. "And the splash from the rock hitting the water scared us so much that none of us dared to sleep that night." Before we went to bed, another immigration police officer pointed toward a place not far from our tent. "If anything happens, climb up this way immediately," he told us. "Grab that metal railing over there." It was the escape route. Our little patch of level ground had been carved out of the mud by hand. However, a downpour that night turned our tent into a small pond. I woke suddenly in the middle of the night, and found there was water everywhere. I shifted my body, pulled the opening of my sleeping bag tightly around me and forced myself to go back to sleep. The next morning, when we got up, the rescuers were already preparing to head out. We emptied the water from our tent and began clearing our things. The clothes we had used as pillows the night before were completely soaked. Seeing this, a firefighter brought us a set of rescue clothes and urged us to put them on. I stepped outside and looked back toward Gyirong Town. Six or seven hundred meters away, excavators were already at work. Another day had begun. In the heart of the disaster zone, rescuers once again scoured areas they had already searched several times for the missing. They were firefighters in orange, immigration police in dark blue uniforms, disinfection workers in disease-control gear, and police officers carrying cameras and notebooks. At first, everyone was searching for survivors. They called out again and again. They turned over debris and dug through the mud, searching every possible place. Then, slowly, painfully, everyone began to confront a reality that no one wanted to accept. At around 10 a.m., rescuers paused their work and stood in silence in a brief memorial service to mourn the victims. Then, they put on their safety helmets and marched again into the mud. ■

item.title: Xi's cultural journey through museums
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
CAIRO, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- On the Giza Plateau, the majestic pyramids, silent witnesses to millennia of history, now gaze across at the Grand Egyptian Museum. Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, visited the museum on Wednesday during his state visit to Egypt, where they were warmly received by Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi and his wife. Surrounded by ancient artifacts, the two presidential couples toured the grand galleries, posing for a photo before a towering statue of Ramses II, one of the most famous pharaohs of Egypt, as curators delivered a swift primer on pharaonic history. "This museum is a book with endless pages," Xi said. He, during the tour, also urged the two countries to promote the inclusive coexistence and mutual learning among different civilizations, and pool greater strength from civilizations to advance the building of a community with a shared future for humanity. As the world's largest museum dedicated to a single civilization, the Grand Egyptian Museum houses more than 100,000 precious artifacts. Locals have newly dubbed it the "fourth pyramid of Giza." The Grand Egyptian Museum is just one of the many museums Xi has visited over the years. Whether on domestic inspection tours or overseas trips, his visits have taken him to the Sanxingdui Museum in southwest China's Sichuan province and the Yinxu Museum in central China's Henan province, key sites of early Chinese civilization, as well as the Amir Timur Museum in Uzbekistan, and the ancient Maya ruins of Chichen Itza in Mexico. The list goes on. Such frequent museum visits stem from Xi's longstanding emphasis on preserving and carrying forward traditional culture. For Xi, museums are important places that protect and pass on human civilizations. In November 2019, during his visit to the Acropolis Museum in Athens, Greece, Xi paused to admire the relief of the "Pensive Athena," the Greek goddess of war and wisdom. He and then Greek President Prokopis Pavlopoulos explored how ancient Chinese and Greek civilizations expressed their reflections on war and their shared longing for peace. Museums have also been a frequent choice for Xi to present traditional Chinese culture when hosting foreign dignitaries. During U.S. President Donald Trump's two visits to China in 2017 and 2026, Xi hosted him at the Forbidden City, or the Palace Museum, and the Temple of Heaven, respectively, using the historic sites to illustrate the Chinese philosophy of pursuing peace and harmony. In Xi's eyes, museums are not simply repositories of the past. They offer people a chance to discover unfamiliar histories, recognize common threads of human creativity and gain a deeper understanding of one another. During his first state visit to Egypt in 2016, Xi toured Luxor, a city widely known as one of the world's largest open-air museums. Walking along the main avenue of Luxor Temple, Xi and Sisi discussed the distinctive features of their two ancient civilizations, recalling their long history of exchanges and mutual learning. At the temple, they also witnessed the launch of the 2016 China-Egypt Culture Year, a landmark moment in bilateral cultural exchanges. Today, the Grand Egyptian Museum provides a new setting for that dialogue between the two ancient civilizations. In a message to Sisi on its opening last year, Xi said that the museum will leave a profound mark on Egypt's cultural history and play an important role in preserving and passing on the ancient Egyptian civilization. It is encouraging to see the two ancient civilizations reaching out to each other, with the two peoples growing ever closer through mutual understanding and affinity, Xi said in the message. From Beijing to Cairo, Xi's museum visits underscore how history can bridge rather than divide civilizations, enabling them to deepen mutual understanding and draw on the wisdom of the past to shape the road ahead. As Xi has observed, "Museums bridge the past, present, and future."■

item.title: Xi sends congratulatory message to 8th China-Russia Energy Business Forum
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
BEIJING, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Friday sent a congratulatory message to the 8th China-Russia Energy Business Forum held in Vladivostok, Russia. In the message, Xi noted that this year marks the 30th anniversary of the establishment of the China-Russia strategic partnership of coordination and the 25th anniversary of the signing of the China-Russia Treaty of Good-Neighborliness and Friendly Cooperation. Amid a complex and evolving international situation, he said, the China-Russia comprehensive strategic partnership of coordination for a new era has maintained high-level development, and bilateral energy cooperation has yielded fruitful results, strongly promoting the two countries' common development and becoming an example of mutually beneficial cooperation. Stressing that the global energy landscape is undergoing profound adjustments, with opportunities and challenges intertwined, Xi said China stands ready to work with Russia to continuously deepen energy cooperation and jointly safeguard the stability and smooth operation of energy industrial and supply chains. On Friday, Russian President Vladimir Putin also sent a congratulatory message to the forum. ■

item.title: Xi urges greater efforts to nurture capable young people for socialist cause
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
BEIJING, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Congratulating a popular national children's radio program on its 70th anniversary, Chinese President Xi Jinping urged professionals in children's culture to redouble efforts in nurturing a new generation of capable young people for the socialist cause. Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the call in a congratulatory letter sent Friday to China Media Group's program named Xiaolaba, or Little Trumpet. He praised the program's 70-year commitment to "telling good stories to children," which have accompanied generations of young listeners as they grew up. Xi called on the program's team and professionals in children's culture to fulfill the mission of fostering virtue through education, keep pace with the times, tap deeply into the rich cultural resources, and devote themselves to creating more excellent and popular works that promote the true, the good and the beautiful among children. He urged greater efforts to nurture a new generation of capable young people with sound moral grounding, intellectual ability, physical vigor, aesthetic sensibility, and labor skills, who will be able to contribute to and carry forward the socialist cause. Launched on Sept. 4, 1956, Xiaolaba is the first radio program in the People's Republic of China dedicated to preschool children. It has since grown into a flagship program spanning radio, television, new media and in-school broadcasting. ■
